title: Build nanoGPT: PyTorch Tensors and the First Transformer Component

assumptions.self_reported: Python studied at college; basic Python syntax is familiar.
assumptions.not_assumed: No demonstrated expertise in tensor shapes, autograd, normalization or transformer internals.

source_commits.change: Trainable LayerNorm weight and optional bias

roadmap_note: Original reconstructed commit chronology is preserved as context. One lesson groups related commits; no commit count is used as a pedagogical quota.

text: You know Python from college. We will skip variables, loops and basic functions.
This chapter starts where the real nanoGPT project starts to get interesting: PyTorch tensors and its first reusable neural-network component.
We will group related Git commits, then connect their code to the final model and training pipeline.
slides.title: Build nanoGPT · Your First Model Component

text: nanoGPT is a neural network that predicts the next token from earlier tokens.
It is built from data preparation → token embeddings → transformer blocks → predictions → training → generation.
Our goal today is to understand and test one component that later sits inside every transformer block.
The repository's earliest reconstructed commits assemble model.py: imports, a custom LayerNorm, then attention and other transformer components.
Instead of one commit per lesson, we will combine the first five related commits to build a single tested component.
Later lessons will reuse the same component instead of starting from scratch.

slides.tag: WHERE DOES A MODEL RECEIVE DATA?
text: The dataset script converts Shakespeare characters to integer IDs and saves them. Training reads those IDs into batches.
This is why data preparation and neural-network code depend on each other.
slides.code:
train_ids = encode(train_data)
train_ids = np.array(train_ids, dtype=np.uint16)

text: The real training code creates x and y: input tokens and next-token targets.
If the input is [3, 1, 4], the target for the same window might be [1, 4, 2].
These are numbers, not yet vectors of learned features.
slides.code:
x = torch.tensor([[3, 1, 4]])
y = torch.tensor([[1, 4, 2]])
print(x.shape)

text: A PyTorch tensor is a multidimensional container of numbers. Think of an array with a shape and a datatype.
We will work with torch.Tensor rather than re-teaching Python lists.
slides.code:
import torch
x = torch.tensor([[3, 1, 4],
                  [2, 0, 1]])
print(x.shape)

text: What does the shape [2, 3] tell us?
slides.why: The first axis is the number of sequences (batch size); the second is tokens per sequence.

text: The model cannot do useful attention on arbitrary integer token IDs.
An embedding learns a numerical vector for each token. The real code uses nn.Embedding.
slides.note: Teaching simplification; the repository builds this embedding inside an nn.ModuleDict.

text: We'll use a toy vocabulary of 10 IDs, each mapped to 8 learned features.
The integer inputs have shape [2,4]; the embedding output adds a feature dimension.
slides.code:
import torch
from torch import nn
embed = nn.Embedding(10, 8)
ids = torch.tensor([[1, 2, 3, 4],
                    [4, 3, 2, 1]])
x = embed(ids)
print(x.shape)

text: Why does the embedding output have 3 dimensions?
choices: Each token gets an 8-number feature vector
slides.why: The embedding looks up one feature vector for every token ID. So [B,T] becomes [B,T,C].

text: The repository labels hidden-state dimensions as B, T, C.
B = batch size, T = sequence length, C = embedding or feature channels (n_embd).
In the toy example, B=2, T=4, C=8.
slides.code:
B, T, C = x.shape
print(B, T, C)

text: If a hidden-state tensor has shape [2,4,8], which is n_embd?
slides.why: n_embd is the number of learned features per token, the last axis C=8.

text: Each token now has a vector of feature values. Their scale can vary while passing through many layers.
Layer normalization makes the features at each token more consistently scaled, helping the network optimize.
It preserves the number of tokens and channels.
slides.code:
x.shape  # [B, T, C]
# LayerNorm normalizes along C

text: The early commit sequence introduces the Python module, imports, the LayerNorm class, its learnable parameters, and the forward computation.
These changes form one component, so we will study them together.
The original file imports torch, torch.nn and the functional API F.
nn contains modules and learnable parameters. F provides operations such as layer_norm.
slides.code:
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
from torch.nn import functional as F

text: The project defines LayerNorm as an nn.Module subclass.
A module can own trainable parameters and define a forward() computation.
weight starts as ones. It is an nn.Parameter, so PyTorch registers it for learning.
Each channel has its own learnable scale value.
Why use nn.Parameter(...) for the scale?
choices: To mark the tensor as trainable module state
slides.why: Registered nn.Parameters are visible to module.parameters() and can be updated by an optimizer.

text: The original implementation allows a learnable bias vector to be turned on or off.
When bias=False, self.bias is None. It is not a vector of zeros that the optimizer still trains.
What is stored in self.bias when the constructor receives bias=False?
slides.why: The conditional expression chooses None when bias=False, so no bias Parameter is registered.

text: The forward() method calls F.layer_norm.
The second argument, self.weight.shape, identifies the feature dimension(s) to normalize.
The small epsilon protects against division by zero.
For a token feature vector [1,2,3,4], the mean is 2.5.
LayerNorm subtracts the mean and divides by the standard deviation (with epsilon for stability). With initial scale=1 and bias=0, the result is approximately:
slides.code:
x = torch.tensor([[[1., 2., 3., 4.]]])
y = F.layer_norm(x, (4,))
print(y.flatten().tolist())
slides.note: Rounded values; actual print includes more decimal places.

text: Given [B,T,C]=[2,4,8] and LayerNorm(8), which values are normalized together?
choices: All 64 numbers in the batch at once
The 8 channels for each token independently
Only the first token of each sequence
slides.why: LayerNorm(8) normalizes each length-8 feature vector independently across the final dimension.

text: What is the output shape after LayerNorm(8) receives torch.randn(2,4,8)?
slides.why: Layer normalization changes numeric values, not the dimensions of its input tensor.

text: Here is the core component assembled from those five commits. The excerpt is the repository's real implementation with its explanatory comment removed.
We can now instantiate it and test it independently.
The practice script will import LayerNorm from the repository's actual model.py.
We generate a batch of toy hidden states, run the layer, and assert that the shape is preserved.
slides.code:
from model import LayerNorm
x = torch.randn(2, 4, 8)
ln = LayerNorm(ndim=8, bias=False)
y = ln(x)
assert y.shape == x.shape
assert ln.bias is None
slides.note: The downloadable practice script handles the Python import path from its learning/ folder.

text: What should you find in dict(ln.named_parameters()) when ln = LayerNorm(8, False)?
slides.why: weight is an nn.Parameter. bias is None, so the module has no trainable bias parameter.

text: LayerNorm is not the entire language model. It is inserted into every transformer Block.
The repository uses ln_1 before attention and ln_2 before the feed-forward MLP.
slides.code:
self.ln_1 = LayerNorm(config.n_embd, bias=config.bias)
self.attn = CausalSelfAttention(config)
self.ln_2 = LayerNorm(config.n_embd, bias=config.bias)
self.mlp = MLP(config)

text: The block's forward method combines normalized inputs with attention and then an MLP.
The additions are residual connections: they combine an input with the output of a sub-layer.
We will implement attention and MLP in upcoming chapters; for now recognize where your LayerNorm executes.
slides.code:
def forward(self, x):
    x = x + self.attn(self.ln_1(x))
    x = x + self.mlp(self.ln_2(x))
    return x

text: Which call runs immediately before attention in the real Block.forward?
slides.why: The source calls self.attn(self.ln_1(x)): first normalize, then run attention.

text: The GPT model creates token and position embeddings, a list of transformer blocks, and a final LayerNorm.
Your small layer is reused many times. The full model is connected rather than a collection of isolated snippets.
slides.code:
wte = nn.Embedding(config.vocab_size, config.n_embd)
wpe = nn.Embedding(config.block_size, config.n_embd)
h = nn.ModuleList([Block(config) for _ in range(config.n_layer)])
ln_f = LayerNorm(config.n_embd, bias=config.bias)

text: The real model converts token IDs to vectors, adds position vectors, runs transformer blocks, then normalizes again.
Your LayerNorm eventually operates on x in this path.
slides.code:
tok_emb = self.transformer.wte(idx)
pos_emb = self.transformer.wpe(pos)
x = self.transformer.drop(tok_emb + pos_emb)
for block in self.transformer.h:
    x = block(x)
x = self.transformer.ln_f(x)

text: The training script constructs the GPT configuration and model using the parameters read from its config.
That is where n_embd and bias reach the LayerNorm constructor. Data batches flow into this model in a later stage.
slides.code:
model_args = dict(n_layer=n_layer, n_head=n_head,
                  n_embd=n_embd, block_size=block_size,
                  bias=bias, vocab_size=None, dropout=dropout)
gptconf = GPTConfig(**model_args)
model = GPT(gptconf)

text: Where does the config.n_embd used by LayerNorm ultimately come from in a training run?
choices: The model configuration used to construct GPT
slides.why: Training builds GPTConfig from model_args. GPT passes config to Blocks and LayerNorm.

text: A hidden-state tensor is shaped [2,4,8], but a developer accidentally writes LayerNorm(4, True).
What is the mismatch?
slides.code:
x = torch.randn(2, 4, 8)
ln = LayerNorm(4, True)
y = ln(x)
choices: The normalized_shape should match the final 8 features
The layer only works on a GPU
slides.why: LayerNorm normalizes the final C dimension; here C=8 but the module was configured for 4.

text: Configure the layer with ndim=8 to match the last dimension.
This kind of shape reasoning will matter throughout queries, keys, values and the full transformer.
slides.code:
x = torch.randn(2, 4, 8)
ln = LayerNorm(8, True)
y = ln(x)
print(tuple(y.shape))

text: The exercise file in this lesson uses the actual model.LayerNorm.
Run it, switch bias=False to True, and inspect named_parameters().
The answer matters because every Block constructs its LayerNorm from the configuration's bias flag.
The layer starts with weight=1 and bias=0 (if enabled). What can happen during model training?
choices: The scale and optional bias can be updated by the optimizer
The tensor must change its shape
slides.why: Because weight and optional bias are registered nn.Parameters, training can update them.

text: The first five related commits created the module and a reusable LayerNorm implementation.
We studied those commits as one feature, then traced it into later code in the same project.
Next we will use the same tensor shapes to build causal attention—not repeat Python basics.
You've connected real source lines across data/shakespeare_char/prepare.py, train.py and model.py.
You can now explain tensor shapes, embeddings, registered parameters, LayerNorm's math and where this class runs in GPT.

steps: Run from repository root with Python and torch installed.
Check model.LayerNorm shape preservation and normalized per-token mean/variance.
Toggle bias=True/False and inspect registered parameters.
Create a wrong LayerNorm dimension to observe the mismatch.
lab.expected: Shape (2,4,8), normalized features near zero mean, bias registered only when enabled.
